paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive syndromic disorder in which seizures begin in the first months of life. The seizures are mainly epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures, and EEG shows a suppression-burst pattern or hypsarrhythmia. Affected individuals have hypotonia and severe developmental impairment. Non-neural features vary between patients and include cleft palate, joint contractures, pes equinovarus, omphalocele, other skeletal abnormalities, and dysmorphic facial features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian, and Brazilian origin with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. paragraphs.text: In family A of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were healthy first cousins of Algerian origin. Their first child (case 1) was a 6-year-old boy. When first referred at 5 months of age, he had developmental regression with loss of visual contact, opisthotonus, and axial hypotonia. He had epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia, followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizures after age 3 years, and his epilepsy was drug-resistant. At 6 years he had spastic tetraparesis, limited extension of the knees and elbows, scoliosis, plagiocephaly, and profound intellectual disability. He had no verbal communication and could not sit unassisted. He had a cleft soft palate, and brain MRI was normal. His sister (case 2) was born at 37 weeks' gestation. At 2 days of age she was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for episodes of eye revulsion, cyanosis, and spasm-like movements, and EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern. At 26 months she had severe developmental delay, axial hypotonia, no head control, segmental hypertonia with limited extension of the knees, no visual contact, abnormal eye movements, no verbal communication, and profound intellectual disability. She also had a cleft soft palate.

paragraphs.text: In family B of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were first cousins of Egyptian origin. Their third child (case 3), a girl, was born after a pregnancy with polyhydramnios. At birth she had an omphalocele and a cleft soft palate, as well as jejunal atresia, right talipes equinovarus, and a branchial fistula. From 2 weeks of age she had epileptic spasms and eye twitches. Her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern that evolved to hypsarrhythmia. She had severe developmental delay, profound intellectual disability, spasticity, and failure to thrive. Her dysmorphic features included: - plagiocephaly with bitemporal narrowing, forehead nevus flammeus, and facial hirsutism - midface hypoplasia, facial asymmetry, and microretrognathia - bluish sclerae, large corneas, squint, hypertelorism, and downslanting palpebral fissures - a broad depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, and a smooth long philtrum - low-set abnormally shaped ears, a thin upper lip vermilion, delayed tooth eruption, and a high-arched palate She also had multiple skin hemangiomas, a short neck with anterior webbing, and axillary webbing. Movement was limited in all joints, and she had ulnar deviation at the wrists, camptodactyly, adducted thumbs, and rocker-bottom feet. Other findings were a short thorax with hypoplastic, widely spaced nipples, scoliosis, and a large clitoris with hypoplastic labia. Brain MRI showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum, progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and mildly enlarged lateral ventricles. She died at 2 years of age from a respiratory infection. Her brother (case 4) was similarly affected. At birth he had an omphalocele and bilateral talipes equinovarus, but no cleft palate. He had epileptic spasms and eye twitches with a suppression-burst EEG, arthrogryposis, global developmental delay, profound intellectual disability, hyperreflexia, spasticity, dysmorphic facial features, and failure to thrive. He died at 4 years of age from pulmonary infection and severe growth retardation.

paragraphs.text: In family C of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were first cousins of Turkish origin. Their first child (case 5) was a 12-year-old girl. Eyelid myoclonia began at 2 weeks of age, and a week later she also had myoclonic seizures of the upper limbs. She later had generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and her epilepsy was refractory. EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern, multifocal spike-wave complexes, and photosensitivity. She had generalized hypotonia in infancy and later developed tetraparesis with increased muscle tone. She had profound intellectual disability, no expressive or receptive speech, and no head control. Other features were a cleft palate, left talipes, conductive hearing loss, and recurrent fever without infection. She had no facial dysmorphism, and brain MRI was normal. Her brother (case 6) had a similar phenotype. From the first day of life he had refractory myoclonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic seizures, and EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern. Like his sister, he had a cleft palate. His seizures worsened on a ketogenic diet. He died from refractory seizures at 2 years of age, when he had profound intellectual disability and tetraparesis with increased muscle tone. His brain MRI was normal.

paragraphs.text: In family D of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were healthy second cousins from Iran, and there was a family history of epilepsy and developmental delay. Their second child (case 7), a boy, had myoclonic seizures within 1 day of birth, with EEG dysrhythmia, and the seizures evolved into epileptic spasms. His neurodevelopment was profoundly delayed: he was unable to walk and had profound intellectual disability. He was initially hypotonic and later developed spasticity, dystonia, and scoliosis. Brain imaging showed prominent inner liquor spaces. His facial features were low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, mild hypertelorism, and a thin upper lip. His sister (case 8) was born at 38 weeks' gestation by cesarean section. At 7 days of age she had epileptic spasms and myoclonic seizures, with a burst-attenuation EEG pattern. At 15 months she could roll onto her sides but could not sit unsupported. Her head circumference was 44 cm, 1.2 cm below the 3rd centile. She also had axial hypotonia, mild dystonia, and profound intellectual disability. Neither sib had cleft palate or pes equinovarus.

paragraphs.text: In family E of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were first cousins of Turkish origin. Their second child (case 9), a boy, had intrauterine hydrocephalus. He was referred at 2 months of age for facial dysmorphism, developmental delay, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, and pes equinovarus. Epileptic spasms were seen on examination. In retrospect they had been present from 1 month of age, but the parents had not recognized them as seizures. EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. He also had: - facial features: high-arched eyebrows, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, a long philtrum, thin lips, low-set ears, an auricular pit, and microretrognathia - cervical and axillary webbing, flexion contractures of the elbows and knees, ulnar deviation of the wrists, and an atlantoaxial anomaly - rectus diastasis, an umbilical hernia, a palpable liver, and hirsutism of the back - eye findings: nystagmus, alternating esotropia, and bilateral pale optic discs - a failed hearing test at 1 year - recurrent aspiration pneumonia - a small patent foramen ovale and atrial septal defect, and focal septal hypertrophy - grade 1 nephrocalcinosis - length below the 3rd centile, a large anterior fontanel, and sparse hair and eyebrows - neurologic findings: no head control or eye contact, axial hypotonia, limb spasticity, and profound intellectual disability His sib (case 10), a boy, was born at 29 weeks' gestation. He had a cleft palate, short neck, narrow thorax, myoclonic seizures, pes equinovarus, hypertelorism, macrocephaly, short limbs, abdominal distension, and germinal matrix hemorrhage. His heart findings were a large patent ductus arteriosus, a small atrial septal defect, and moderate pulmonary hypertension. He died of sepsis on postnatal day 9.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients from 6 families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian, and Turkish ancestry with early-infantile onset epilepsy and developmental delay. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age in all 6 patients and were controlled with medication in 3. All patients had intellectual disability despite seizure control, which suggested to the authors that the genetic defect affected development independently of seizure control. Non-CNS features varied and included skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features, and cleft palate.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) studied 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families with DEE89 by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. They identified homozygous mutations in the GAD1 gene as the only likely pathogenic variants, and Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with the disease. The mutations were: - family A (Algerian): a splice site mutation (c.1414-1G-C), predicted in silico to abolish the acceptor splice site of exon 15 - family B (Egyptian): an in-frame 3-bp deletion in exon 7 (c.695_697delAGA), removing a highly conserved lysine (lys232del) - family C (Turkish): a 5-bp deletion (c.812_816delTTAAG), causing a frameshift (Val271AspfsTer9) - families D (Iranian) and E (Turkish): the same nonsense mutation, c.1591C-T, resulting in an arg531-to-ter (R531X) substitution - family F (Brazilian): a missense mutation resulting in a glu509-to-lys (E509K) substitution, absent from the gnomAD database In 4 families the mutations were predicted to truncate the protein, which supported a complete loss-of-function mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) studied the c.1414-1G-C mutation in cDNA from the heterozygous parents in family A. The mutant allele produced no normal mRNA but gave 3 aberrant isoforms: one skipping exon 15, one retaining 76 bases of intron 14, and one lacking the first 7 bases of exon 15. In a cell-free expression system, the lys232del protein was expressed at levels comparable to wildtype, so loss of function could not be formally shown. The authors noted that this assay bypasses splicing and that in silico tools predicted an effect on splicing. They considered the knockout mouse-like phenotype of cleft palate plus omphalocele in family B strongly supportive of pathogenicity. A structural model of GAD67 predicted that the E509K substitution, at a highly conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain, would disrupt salt bridges with arg316, lys318, and lys389. The model also predicted that the larger, positively charged lysine side chain would not fit into the domain core.

Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with the disease. Because the 2 families come from neighboring regions, the authors suggested that the mutation may lie on a shared ancestral haplotype. The phenotype differed between the 2 families: those in family D had no cleft palate or pes equinovarus, whereas those in family E had both.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported a 7-year-old Brazilian girl with DEE89 (case 11) whose parents were first cousins (family F). She was homozygous for a c.1525G-A transition in the GAD1 gene, resulting in a glu509-to-lys (E509K) substitution. The mutation was absent from gnomAD, and Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with the disease. Structural modeling placed the substitution at a highly conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain. The model predicted that it would disrupt salt bridges with arg316, lys318, and lys389, and that the larger, positively charged lysine side chain would not fit into the domain core.
